title: How to Calculate PF (Provident Fund) on Salary: Formula, Examples & New Rules 2026
summary: Learn how to calculate PF on salary with step-by-step formula, 4 worked examples, employer/employee split, Rs 15,000 wage ceiling, VPF, tax benefits, and 2026 labour code changes. Complete EPF guide for Indian employers and HR.
body_text: Insights & Resources How to Calculate PF (Provident Fund) on Salary: Formula, Examples & New Rules 2026 July 24, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet What Is PF (Provident Fund)? Provident Fund (PF) — formally known as the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) — is India’s most important retirement savings scheme for salaried workers. Managed by the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) under the Code on Social Security, 2020 (which consolidated the earlier EPF & MP Act, 1952), it creates a mandatory savings pool that grows throughout an employee’s career. The core mechanism is straightforward: both the employer and the employee contribute 12% each of the employee’s basic salary plus dearness allowance (DA) every month. The employee’s entire 12% goes into the EPF account, while the employer’s 12% is split between the EPF account and the Employee Pension Scheme (EPS). The accumulated corpus earns compound interest — currently 8.25% per annum for FY 2025–26 — and is available for withdrawal at retirement, or partially for specific life events like buying a house, medical emergencies, or children’s education. For employers, understanding PF calculation is not optional. Incorrect contributions attract penalties, interest on delayed payments, and even prosecution under the EPF Act. For employees, knowing how PF works helps in salary negotiation, tax planning, and retirement readiness. Who Is Covered Under EPF? EPF coverage depends on the size of the establishment and the salary level of the employee. Here are the current rules: • Mandatory coverage: Every establishment employing 20 or more persons is required to register under the EPF scheme. This includes factories, shops, educational institutions, hospitals, and service organisations. • Voluntary registration: Establishments with fewer than 20 employees can voluntarily register. Once registered, the EPF provisions become mandatory. • Employee eligibility: All employees drawing a basic salary plus DA of up to Rs 15,000 per month are mandatorily enrolled in EPF from the date of joining. • Higher-salaried employees: Employees earning above Rs 15,000 basic + DA are not mandatorily required to join. However, if they are already EPF members (from a previous job, for instance), they continue as members. Many employers also voluntarily cover all employees regardless of salary. • International workers: Employees from countries that do not have a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with India are covered under EPF when working in India, regardless of their salary level. Good to Know Once an employee becomes an EPF member, the membership continues until retirement or withdrawal. Switching jobs does not break membership — the Universal Account Number (UAN) follows the employee across employers. PF Contribution Structure: Employee vs. Employer The table below summarises how EPF contributions are structured. Both sides contribute 12% of basic salary plus DA, but the employer’s share is split between two sub-schemes. Contributor Rate Goes To Calculation Base Employee 12% of Basic + DA 100% to EPF account Basic Salary + DA Employer 12% of Basic + DA Split: 3.67% to EPF + 8.33% to EPS Basic Salary + DA While the total percentage is the same for both sides, the destination of the money differs. The employee’s full 12% sits in the EPF account and earns interest. The employer’s contribution is divided between the employee’s EPF account (3.67%) and a pension fund managed by EPFO (8.33%). Employer’s 12% Split: EPF vs. EPS (Detailed Breakdown) This split is one of the most commonly misunderstood aspects of PF. Let us break it down precisely. Component Rate Cap Purpose Employer EPF 3.67% of Basic + DA No cap Employee’s individual PF account (earns interest) Employer EPS 8.33% of Basic + DA Capped at Rs 15,000 basic = Rs 1,250/month Pension fund (monthly pension post-retirement) The critical point is the EPS cap. Regardless of how high the employee’s basic salary is, the employer’s EPS contribution is calculated on a maximum basic of Rs 15,000. This means the EPS contribution can never exceed Rs 1,250 per month (8.33% of Rs 15,000). When an employee’s basic salary exceeds Rs 15,000, the EPS contribution stays fixed at Rs 1,250, and the remainder of the employer’s 12% (which would have gone to EPS) is redirected to the employee’s EPF account instead. This is a significant advantage for higher-salaried employees because the redirected amount earns interest in their EPF account. Important Exception — Higher Pension Option Employees who joined EPF before 1 September 2014 can opt for EPS contributions on their actual salary (not capped at Rs 15,000). The Supreme Court upheld this right in November 2022. If an employee exercises this option, the employer’s full 8.33% goes to EPS on actual salary, reducing the EPF portion. The deadline for opting in has been extended multiple times by EPFO. PF Calculation Formula The formulas below are what every payroll team needs to know. There are two scenarios depending on whether the employee’s basic salary plus DA is below or above the Rs 15,000 wage ceiling. Employee PF Contribution (Same in Both Scenarios) Employee PF = 12% × (Basic Salary + Dearness Allowance) Employer Contribution When Basic + DA ≤ Rs 15,000 Employer EPF = 3.67% × (Basic + DA) Employer EPS = 8.33% × (Basic + DA) Total Employer Contribution = 12% × (Basic + DA) Employer Contribution When Basic + DA > Rs 15,000 Employer EPS = 8.33% × Rs 15,000 = Rs 1,250 (FIXED) Employer EPF = [12% × (Basic + DA)] – Rs 1,250 Total Employer Contribution = 12% × (Basic + DA) Notice that the total employer contribution remains 12% of basic + DA in both cases. Only the internal split between EPF and EPS changes once the salary crosses Rs 15,000. The Rs 15,000 PF Wage Ceiling Explained The Rs 15,000 figure appears frequently in PF discussions, but it serves two different purposes, and conflating them causes confusion: 1. Mandatory Membership Threshold: Employees earning basic + DA up to Rs 15,000 per month must be enrolled in EPF. Those earning above this threshold are not mandatorily required to join (but can do so voluntarily, and existing members continue). 2. EPS Contribution Cap: The employer’s pension (EPS) contribution is always calculated on a maximum basic of Rs 15,000, regardless of actual salary. This caps EPS at Rs 1,250 per month. Capped PF vs. Full-Basic PF Many companies give employees earning above Rs 15,000 the option to either: • Cap PF at Rs 15,000: Both employee and employer contribute 12% on Rs 15,000 only. Employee PF deduction = Rs 1,800/month. This maximises take-home pay. • Contribute PF on full basic: Both sides contribute 12% on the actual basic salary. Higher PF deduction, lower take-home, but significantly larger retirement corpus. Neither option is universally better. Employees who prioritise immediate cash flow prefer the capped approach. Those focused on long-term savings and tax benefits (under Section 80C) prefer full-basic PF. We will illustrate the difference with numbers in Example 4. Worked Examples: PF Calculation Step by Step Let us work through four real-world scenarios to make the formulas concrete. All figures are monthly. Example 1: Basic Salary = Rs 12,000 (Below the Rs 15,000 Ceiling) This employee’s basic + DA is below the wage ceiling, so the standard split applies directly. Component Calculation Amount Employee PF (12%) 12% × Rs 12,000 Rs 1,440 Employer EPF (3.67%) 3.67% × Rs 12,000 Rs 440 Employer EPS (8.33%) 8.33% × Rs 12,000 Rs 1,000 Total EPF Credit (Employee + Employer EPF) Rs 1,440 + Rs 440 Rs 1,880 Key Takeaway The Rs 1,000 EPS contribution goes to the pension fund and does not appear in the employee’s EPF passbook. The withdrawable PF balance grows by Rs 1,880 each month. Example 2: Basic Salary = Rs 15,000 (At the Ceiling) At exactly Rs 15,000, the employee is at the upper boundary. The EPS cap equals the actual calculation, so no adjustment is needed. Component Calculation Amount Employee PF (12%) 12% × Rs 15,000 Rs 1,800 Employer EPF (3.67%) 3.67% × Rs 15,000 Rs 551 Employer EPS (8.33%) 8.33% × Rs 15,000 Rs 1,250 Total EPF Credit (Employee + Employer EPF) Rs 1,800 + Rs 551 Rs 2,351 Verification: Employer EPF (Rs 551) + Employer EPS (Rs 1,250) = Rs 1,801. The 1-rupee rounding difference arises because 3.67% + 8.33% = 12.00%, and 12% of Rs 15,000 = Rs 1,800. EPFO rounds to the nearest rupee for each component separately. Example 3: Basic Salary = Rs 30,000 (PF on Full Basic, Above Ceiling) This employee’s company contributes PF on the full basic salary. Since the basic exceeds Rs 15,000, the EPS cap kicks in. Component Calculation Amount Employee PF (12%) 12% × Rs 30,000 Rs 3,600 Employer Total (12%) 12% × Rs 30,000 Rs 3,600 Employer EPS (capped) 8.33% × Rs 15,000 Rs 1,250 Employer EPF (remainder) Rs 3,600 – Rs 1,250 Rs 2,350 Total EPF Credit (Employee + Employer EPF) Rs 3,600 + Rs 2,350 Rs 5,950 Because the EPS is capped, the employer’s additional Rs 2,350 flows into the EPF account, earning 8.25% interest. This is money the employee would not receive if their company capped PF at Rs 15,000. Example 4: Basic Salary = Rs 50,000 — Capped vs. Full-Basic PF Comparison This is the scenario that matters most during salary negotiation. Let us compare both approaches side by side. Component PF Capped at Rs 15,000 PF on Full Basic (Rs 50,000) Employee PF 12% × Rs 15,000 = Rs 1,800 12% × Rs 50,000 = Rs 6,000 Employer Total 12% × Rs 15,000 = Rs 1,800 12% × Rs 50,000 = Rs 6,000 Employer EPS Rs 1,250 (capped) Rs 1,250 (capped) Employer EPF Rs 1,800 – Rs 1,250 = Rs 550 Rs 6,000 – Rs 1,250 = Rs 4,750 Total Monthly EPF Credit Rs 1,800 + Rs 550 = Rs 2,350 Rs 6,000 + Rs 4,750 = Rs 10,750 Monthly Take-Home Reduction Rs 1,800 Rs 6,000 Annual EPF Accumulation Rs 28,200 Rs 1,29,000 The difference is dramatic: full-basic PF accumulates Rs 1,29,000 per year in the EPF account compared to just Rs 28,200 under the capped approach. Over a 25-year career at 8.25% compound interest, the full-basic approach would build a substantially larger retirement corpus — though at the cost of Rs 4,200 less take-home pay each month. New Rules 2026: How Labour Codes Impact PF Calculation The Code on Social Security, 2020, along with the Code on Wages, 2019, introduced several changes that are reshaping PF calculations as companies comply with the new framework. Here are the seven most important developments: 1. The 50% Basic Wage Rule: Under the new wage definition, basic salary plus DA must constitute at least 50% of the Cost to Company (CTC). Companies that previously structured salaries with a low basic (say 30–40% of CTC) to minimise PF liability must now restructure. The result: the PF calculation base increases, leading to higher PF deductions and a larger retirement corpus, but lower immediate take-home pay. 2. Universal Wage Definition: The Code on Wages defines “wages” as basic pay plus DA plus retaining allowance. All other components (HRA, conveyance, special allowance, etc.) are treated as exclusions. However, if the total value of exclusions exceeds 50% of the total remuneration, the excess amount is reclassified as “wages” and becomes subject to PF contribution. This prevents salary structuring designed to artificially reduce the PF base. 3. Fixed-Term Employees Covered from Day 1: Fixed-term employees (project-based, seasonal, or contractual) now receive the same PF benefits as permanent employees from their first day of employment. There is no minimum service period or waiting period for PF coverage. 4. Social Security for Gig Workers: The Code mandates the Central Government to frame social security schemes for gig workers and platform workers (ride-hailing drivers, delivery personnel, freelancers on platforms). While a PF-equivalent scheme for gig workers has not yet been finalised, it is expected to include a savings-linked benefit similar to EPF. 5. Higher Pension Option Under EPS: Employees who joined EPF before 1 September 2014 can opt for pension contributions on their actual salary rather than the Rs 15,000 cap. The Supreme Court upheld this right in November 2022. EPFO has been processing applications, and the deadline for opting in has been extended multiple times. Employees who exercise this option will see a larger pension in retirement but a smaller EPF balance (since more of the employer’s 12% flows to EPS instead of EPF). 6. EPF Interest Rate Steady at 8.25%: The EPFO has maintained the EPF interest rate at 8.25% per annum for FY 2025–26, the same as the previous year. This rate remains one of the highest among guaranteed-return savings instruments in India, making EPF an attractive retirement vehicle. 7. Tax on High PF Contributions: Interest earned on employee PF contributions exceeding Rs 2.5 lakh per year (or Rs 5 lakh if the employer does not contribute to EPF) is now taxable. This primarily affects high-salaried employees who contribute PF on their full basic salary. For example, an employee with a basic salary of Rs 2,50,000 per month contributes Rs 30,00,000 annually to PF — interest on the amount above Rs 2.5 lakh is added to taxable income. Action Point for Employers If your company has not yet restructured salary components to comply with the 50% basic rule, now is the time. Non-compliance can lead to penalties under both the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security. SalaryBox can help you model the impact on each employee’s take-home pay before you make the switch. VPF: Voluntary Provident Fund Beyond the mandatory 12%, employees have the option to contribute additional amounts to their provident fund through the Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF) scheme. Here is what you need to know: • Contribution range: An employee can contribute anywhere from 12% (the mandatory minimum) up to 100% of their basic salary plus DA towards PF. The portion above 12% is the VPF contribution. • Employer matching: The employer is not required to match VPF contributions. The employer’s obligation is limited to 12% of basic + DA. • Interest rate: VPF earns the same interest rate as EPF — currently 8.25% per annum. This makes it one of the best risk-free investment options available to salaried employees. • Tax benefits: VPF contributions qualify for Section 80C deduction (under the old tax regime) up to the overall limit of Rs 1.5 lakh per annum. Under the new tax regime, Section 80C is not available. • Lock-in: VPF has the same withdrawal rules as EPF. It is not a liquid investment. Contributions are locked until retirement, unemployment, or specific partial withdrawal events. • Ideal for: Employees who want guaranteed, tax-efficient returns without the complexity of choosing mutual funds or other instruments. Particularly attractive for risk-averse individuals close to the Section 80C limit. VPF vs. PPF Both offer similar interest rates and tax benefits, but VPF contributions are deducted directly from salary (convenient and disciplined), while PPF requires manual deposits. VPF also has no separate annual contribution cap beyond the 100%-of-basic limit. PPF is capped at Rs 1.5 lakh per year. PF Withdrawal Rules EPF is designed as a retirement corpus, but the rules allow access under specific circumstances. Understanding these rules helps employees make informed decisions about their PF balance. Full Withdrawal • On retirement: At age 58, the employee can withdraw the entire EPF balance (employee share + employer EPF share + accumulated interest). • On unemployment: If an employee is unemployed for two or more continuous months after leaving a job, they can apply for full withdrawal. • Important: Full withdrawal before completing 5 years of continuous EPF service has tax implications (covered in the next section). Partial Withdrawal (Advances) EPF allows partial withdrawals for specific purposes, subject to minimum service requirements: • Home purchase or construction: Up to 36 months’ basic + DA after 5 years of service. • Home loan repayment: Up to 36 months’ basic + DA after 3 years of service. • Medical emergency: Up to 6 months’ basic + DA (no minimum service period). • Marriage: Up to 50% of employee’s EPF share after 7 years of service (for self, children, or siblings). • Education: Up to 50% of employee’s EPF share after 7 years of service (for self or children). PF Transfer on Job Change When switching jobs, employees should transfer their PF balance to the new employer’s account rather than withdrawing it. The process is entirely online through the EPFO portal using the Universal Account Number (UAN). Benefits of transfer: no tax liability, no break in service period, and the corpus continues to earn interest. PF and Tax Benefits PF enjoys favourable tax treatment at multiple stages. However, recent changes have introduced some tax implications for high earners. Tax Benefits on Contribution • Section 80C deduction (Old Tax Regime): The employee’s PF contribution qualifies for deduction under Section 80C, up to the overall limit of Rs 1.5 lakh per annum. This includes mandatory EPF as well as VPF contributions. • New Tax Regime: Section 80C is not available. PF contributions do not reduce taxable income under the new regime. • Employer’s contribution: Not taxable for the employee. It is the employer’s cost and does not feature in the employee’s taxable salary (up to Rs 7.5 lakh per annum combined with NPS and superannuation). Tax on PF Withdrawal • After 5 years of continuous service: Full withdrawal is completely TAX-FREE. This includes the employee’s contribution, employer’s contribution, and all accumulated interest. • Before 5 years of service: Withdrawal is TAXABLE. The employer’s contribution and interest earned on both contributions are added to the employee’s taxable income for that year. The employee’s own contribution (on which Section 80C was claimed) is also taxed. • Transfer is not withdrawal: Transferring PF from one employer to another is not treated as a withdrawal and has no tax implications. Tax on PF Interest (New Rule) From FY 2021–22 onwards, interest earned on employee PF contributions exceeding Rs 2.5 lakh per year is taxable at the employee’s applicable income tax slab rate. If the employer does not contribute to EPF (only employee contributes), the threshold is Rs 5 lakh per year. This rule primarily affects employees with a monthly basic salary above Rs 2,08,333 who contribute PF on their full basic. EPFO maintains two separate accounts for each member: a non-taxable account (for contributions up to Rs 2.5 lakh) and a taxable account (for excess contributions). Interest on the taxable account is reported in Form 16 and must be included in the income tax return. Additional Employer Charges: EDLI and Admin Beyond the 12% PF contribution, employers bear additional statutory charges. These are not deducted from the employee’s salary — they are entirely the employer’s cost. Charge Rate Cap / Notes EDLI (Employees’ Deposit-Linked Insurance) 0.50% of Basic + DA Calculated on basic capped at Rs 15,000 EPF Admin Charges 0.50% of Basic + DA Minimum Rs 500/month per establishment EDLI Admin Charges Nil Waived since 2015; no charge applicable The EDLI scheme provides life insurance cover to EPF members. In case of death during service, the nominee receives up to Rs 7 lakh (the current maximum benefit under the EDLI scheme). The EPF admin charges fund the operational costs of EPFO. For employers managing payroll manually, tracking these charges alongside the 12% contribution for each employee can be error-prone. A: PF (Provident Fund) is a mandatory retirement savings scheme where both employer and employee contribute 12% of basic salary plus dearness allowance each month. The employee’s 12% goes entirely to the EPF account, while the employer’s 12% is split between EPF (3.67%) and EPS (8.33%). The accumulated corpus earns 8.25% annual interest. Q: What is the PF contribution rate for 2026? A: The PF contribution rate remains 12% each for the employee and employer, calculated on basic salary plus dearness allowance. The EPF interest rate for FY 2025–26 is 8.25% per annum. Q: What is the difference between EPF and EPS? A: EPF (Employees’ Provident Fund) is the employee’s savings account that earns interest and is withdrawable at retirement. EPS (Employee Pension Scheme) is a pension fund from which the employee receives a monthly pension after age 58. The employer’s 12% is split between both: 3.67% to EPF and 8.33% to EPS. Q: What is the PF wage ceiling of Rs 15,000? A: The Rs 15,000 ceiling serves two purposes: (1) employees earning basic + DA up to Rs 15,000 are mandatorily covered under EPF; (2) the employer’s EPS contribution is calculated on a maximum basic of Rs 15,000, capping EPS at Rs 1,250/month regardless of actual salary. Q: How does the 50% basic rule affect PF? A: Under the new labour codes, basic + DA must be at least 50% of CTC. Companies that had lower basic percentages must restructure salaries, which increases the PF calculation base. This means higher PF deductions, lower take-home pay, but a significantly larger retirement fund. Q: Is PF mandatory for all employees? A: PF is mandatory for employees earning basic + DA up to Rs 15,000/month in establishments with 20+ employees. Employees earning above Rs 15,000 are not mandatorily required to join, but existing EPF members continue their membership. Establishments with fewer than 20 employees can opt in voluntarily. Q: What is VPF (Voluntary Provident Fund)? A: VPF allows employees to contribute more than the mandatory 12% of basic + DA to their PF account, up to 100% of basic + DA. VPF earns the same 8.25% interest as EPF and qualifies for Section 80C deduction under the old tax regime. The employer is not required to match VPF contributions. Q: Can I opt out of PF? A: Employees earning basic + DA up to Rs 15,000 cannot opt out of PF. Employees earning above Rs 15,000 who are new to EPF may choose not to join, but those who are already EPF members (from previous employment) generally cannot opt out. Once a member, the membership continues until retirement or qualifying withdrawal. Q: How much interest does PF earn? A: EPF currently earns 8.25% per annum (FY 2025–26). The interest is compounded annually and credited to the EPF account. This rate is declared by EPFO each year and has ranged between 8.10% and 8.65% over the last five years. Q: Is PF withdrawal taxable? A: PF withdrawal after 5 years of continuous service is completely tax-free. Withdrawal before 5 years is taxable: the employer’s contribution, interest, and any Section 80C benefit claimed on the employee’s contribution are added to taxable income. Transferring PF between employers is not a withdrawal and has no tax impact. Q: What are the employer admin charges for PF? A: Employers pay 0.50% of basic + DA as EPF admin charges (minimum Rs 500/month per establishment), and 0.50% of basic + DA (capped at Rs 15,000 basic) for EDLI. EDLI admin charges have been waived since 2015. These charges are the employer’s cost and are not deducted from the employee’s salary. Q: How to calculate PF when salary exceeds Rs 15,000? A: When basic + DA exceeds Rs 15,000 and PF is on full basic: Employee PF = 12% of actual basic. Employer Total = 12% of actual basic. Employer EPS = Rs 1,250 (capped at Rs 15,000). Employer EPF = Employer Total minus Rs 1,250. If PF is capped at Rs 15,000: both employee and employer contribute 12% on Rs 15,000 only (Rs 1,800 each). Provident Fund is more than a payroll deduction — it is the foundation of retirement security for millions of Indian workers. Whether you are an employer ensuring compliance, an HR professional processing payroll, or an employee trying to understand your payslip, getting the PF calculation right matters. The formulas are not complicated, but the details — the EPS cap, the Rs 15,000 ceiling, the capped-versus-full-basic choice, the new 50% rule — require attention. Use the examples in this guide as a reference, and consider automating the process with payroll software like SalaryBox to eliminate manual errors and ensure every rupee is accounted for correctly. title: Meilleurs ETF ESG 2026 : le comparatif complet
summary: Découvrez notre sélection des meilleurs ETF ESG en 2026 : frais, stratégies (SRI, ESG Leaders), éligibilité PEA et zones géographiques comparés en détail.
body_text: Mis à jour le 21 juillet 2026 Les meilleurs ETF ESG combinent un filtre SRI strict ou une méthode ESG Leaders/Selection, des frais sous 0,30 % et une bonne diversification géographique. Cette sélection compare les principaux ETF ESG Monde, USA, Europe et marchés émergents accessibles en France, en PEA ou en compte-titres. L'essentiel Trois stratégies coexistent : exclusion, best-in-class/SRI et thématique, avec des niveaux de sélectivité très différents. Un ETF ESG à réplication physique (Monde, Europe) est rarement éligible au PEA ; la réplication synthétique permet d'y loger une exposition USA ou émergents. Les frais varient de 0,18 % à 0,35 % selon la zone et la méthode de réplication, un écart qui pèse lourd sur 20 ans. Deux ETF “verts” peuvent partager jusqu'à 80 % de leurs positions, ce qui limite la diversification réelle d'un portefeuille combinant plusieurs fonds ESG. Selon la Global Sustainable Investment Alliance, les actifs mondiaux investis selon des critères ESG sont passés de 22 800 à 35 300 milliards de dollars entre 2016 et 2020, avant de refluer à 30 300 milliards de dollars en 2022 sous l'effet d'un durcissement méthodologique aux États-Unis visant à limiter le greenwashing. Les ETF ESG ne s'adressent plus uniquement aux investisseurs idéalistes. Ce segment a atteint une maturité qui propose désormais des solutions d'investissement sophistiquées. Ces produits permettent d'intégrer des critères extra-financiers dans une allocation actions. Qu'est-ce qu'un ETF ESG et comment fonctionne-t-il ? Un ETF ESG réplique un indice actions en appliquant des filtres Environnement, Social et Gouvernance : exclusion de secteurs controversés, sélection des meilleures notes ESG par secteur, ou ciblage d'une thématique précise. Qu'est-ce que l'investissement ESG ? L’investissement ESG ne se limite pas à la performance financière. Il s’agit d’évaluer les entreprises selon trois critères majeurs : Environnement, Social et Gouvernance . Ces critères offrent une perspective plus large que le simple chiffre d’affaires. Aujourd’hui, de plus en plus d’investisseurs s’interrogent sur l’impact de leurs placements. Ils veulent savoir quel est le coût réel pour la planète, les salariés et la société . L’ESG sert de boussole pour mesurer à la fois les risques et les opportunités. On examine l’empreinte carbone, la diversité dans les conseils d’administration, la gestion des déchets ou encore la transparence des rémunérations. L’ESG ne relève pas de la philanthropie . En orientant les flux d’investissement vers les entreprises les plus vertueuses, les ETF ESG encouragent les sociétés à améliorer leurs pratiques. Même un investisseur passif peut ainsi contribuer à des changements concrets. Différentes stratégies ESG (exclusion, best-in-class, ISR, thématique) L’investissement ESG propose plusieurs approches, chacune avec ses spécificités : Exclusion : Cette méthode élimine certains secteurs jugés incompatibles, comme le tabac, les armes ou le charbon. Elle permet d’éviter les activités controversées, mais peut écarter des entreprises en pleine transition. Best-in-class : Cette stratégie sélectionne les entreprises les mieux notées sur les critères ESG dans chaque secteur. Par exemple, une entreprise pétrolière peut intégrer un ETF ESG si elle surpasse ses concurrentes sur le plan environnemental. Cela encourage l’amélioration continue. ISR (Investissement Socialement Responsable) : Cette approche combine exclusions strictes et sélection des meilleurs élèves ESG. ETF thématiques ESG : Ces fonds ciblent des enjeux précis, comme l’eau , les énergies renouvelables ou l’égalité des genres. Ils offrent un impact direct, mais présentent parfois une volatilité plus élevée et une diversification moindre. La clé pour un investisseur ESG averti réside dans la compréhension des critères derrière chaque label . L’ESG ne se résume pas à une simple case à cocher, mais constitue une grille d’analyse exigeante et en constante évolution. Centralisez votre patrimoine PEA, livrets d'épargne, cryptomonnaies, actions, immobilier, comptes bancaires. Découvrir Finary Quels sont les meilleurs ETF ESG à sélectionner en 2026 ? Le choix dépend de la zone géographique visée, du niveau d'exigence ESG recherché et de l'éligibilité au PEA : voici les principaux ETF ESG Monde, USA, Europe, France et marchés émergents disponibles pour un investisseur français. Exemples d'ETF ESG Monde : comparaison et analyse iShares MSCI World SRI UCITS ETF L’iShares MSCI World SRI applique un filtre strict pour ne retenir que le quart le plus vertueux des grandes entreprises mondiales. La sélection exclut massivement des secteurs entiers : tabac, armes, énergies fossiles, OGM, nucléaire. L’ETF exige aussi le respect des principes du Pacte Mondial de l’ONU. Ce processus aboutit à un portefeuille concentré, dominé par la technologie américaine (Microsoft, Nvidia, Tesla). Des géants comme Exxon ou Philip Morris restent exclus, quelle que soit leur capitalisation. Cette approche réduit la diversification sectorielle. La performance peut donc s’écarter sensiblement de l’indice MSCI World classique, surtout lors des hausses des secteurs exclus. Pour les investisseurs recherchant un engagement ESG sans compromis, cet ETF peut constituer une option à étudier . Les frais restent faibles (0,20 %) et la liquidité élevée grâce à un encours de 6,87 Md€ (justETF, 21/07/2026). Amundi MSCI World SRI Climate Paris Aligned UCITS ETF (ex-Amundi World SRI PAB) Amundi propose une alternative souvent un peu moins chère (0,18 % de frais courants). La philosophie reste similaire : sélection SRI stricte, exclusions larges, et concentration sur les leaders ESG de chaque secteur. Les différences concernent surtout les pondérations et un encours plus modeste, mais l’exigence éthique demeure. L’obtention du label ISR français distingue Amundi . Attention : les anciennes parts luxembourgeoises de ce fonds (LU1861134382 et sa version couverte LU2249056297) ont été fusionnées en 2024 dans l'Amundi MSCI World SRI Climate Paris Aligned UCITS ETF Acc, désormais domicilié en Irlande (IE000Y77LGG9), pour les mêmes frais de 0,18 %. Cependant, ni l’iShares ni l’Amundi World SRI ne sont éligibles au PEA, car ils répliquent physiquement un indice mondial. Les investisseurs souhaitant utiliser leur PEA devront se tourner vers la réplication synthétique . Exemples d'ETF ESG USA : comparaison et analyse ETF Amundi PEA MSCI USA ESG Selection UCITS ETF Investir sur le marché américain via le PEA reste complexe en raison de la réglementation. Amundi propose une solution avec un ETF synthétique. Il détient un panier d’actions européennes et réplique la performance d’un indice ESG américain via un swap. Ce montage permet d'utiliser le cadre fiscal du PEA tout en s'exposant aux actions americaines filtrees ESG . La méthodologie “ESG Selection” de MSCI se montre moins stricte que le SRI. Elle sélectionne les entreprises les mieux notées ESG dans chaque secteur, sans exclusions aussi larges. Cette approche offre une meilleure diversification et une performance souvent plus proche de l’indice parent. Les frais sont fixés à 0,35 %, mais l’accès à la tech US (Microsoft, Nvidia, Tesla, Visa) via un PEA séduit de nombreux investisseurs. Le risque de contrepartie lié au swap doit être pris en compte. Les investisseurs les plus prudents doivent en tenir compte . Exemples d'ETF ESG Europe et France ETF Amundi MSCI EMU SRI Climate Paris Aligned UCITS ETF DR L’Europe, pionnière de la finance durable, constitue un terrain privilégié pour les ETF ESG à réplication physique. L’Amundi MSCI EMU SRI Climate Paris Aligned (ex-Amundi EMU SRI) se distingue par : Des frais très bas (0,18 %) Des exclusions strictes (fossiles, nucléaire, tabac) Une sélection des champions ESG de la zone euro (Nokia, ASML, Schneider Electric, AXA, Dassault Systèmes) Cet ETF parvient à combiner engagement ESG et diversification sectorielle. L’industrie, la finance et la technologie y occupent une place importante, sans la surpondération de la tech américaine. Pour les investisseurs recherchant à la fois convictions et stabilité, cet ETF présente un profil diversifié . BNP Paribas Easy Low Carbon 100 Europe PAB UCITS ETF Cet ETF se démarque par son approche résolument climatique : il s’expose à 100 grandes entreprises européennes affichant un bilan CO₂ parmi les plus bas de leur secteur, tout en répondant aux critères stricts du Paris Aligned Benchmark (PAB). On y retrouve de grands noms comme ASML, Novartis ou AstraZeneca, avec un accent sur la santé, la finance ou la consommation durable. Ce tracker thématique permet ainsi de viser une exposition à moindre intensité carbone , via des entreprises sélectionnées selon le Paris Aligned Benchmark. À noter : il n’est pas éligible au PEA (présence d’actions UK/CH) et propose des frais de 0,30%. Envie d'aller plus loin dans l'investissement durable ? Découvrez notre sélection des meilleurs ETF climat pour verdir encore davantage votre portefeuille. ETF Amundi CAC 40 ESG UCITS ETF DR Le CAC 40 ESG reflète la volonté de la France d’intégrer des critères environnementaux et sociaux dans son économie. Cet indice sélectionne 40 entreprises parmi les 60 plus grandes capitalisations françaises. Il exclut les secteurs les plus controversés, comme les armes, le charbon et le tabac, puis pondère les sociétés selon leurs scores ESG. Des groupes majeurs comme LVMH, Schneider Electric, Sanofi et Airbus dominent la composition. L’industrie et la consommation de luxe occupent une place importante. Les frais restent raisonnables (0,25 %) et l’encours affiche une bonne solidité. Pour un investisseur qui souhaite privilégier des valeurs françaises responsables sans renoncer à la performance, cet ETF peut figurer parmi les options à considérer. Exemples d'ETF ESG marchés émergents : comparaison et analyse ETF Amundi PEA Emergent (MSCI Emerging) ESG Transition UCITS ETF Acc Les marchés émergents reçoivent souvent des critiques sur leur engagement ESG, notamment pour leur manque de rigueur ou des pratiques de greenwashing. L’ETF Amundi PEA Emergent ESG Transition propose une sélection des entreprises les mieux notées ESG dans chaque pays, tout en limitant la pondération de chaque émetteur à 5 %. La réplication synthétique rend cet ETF éligible au PEA, mais introduit un risque de contrepartie. La composition met en avant la Chine, Taïwan, l’Inde et la Corée. Les géants de la tech et de la finance émergente côtoient des industriels en transformation. Les frais sont corrects, surtout que l’accès à la croissance émergente filtrée par l’ESG reste rare dans l’univers PEA. Découvrir Finary Comment bien choisir son ETF ESG ? Les critères déterminants sont les frais (TER), l'historique de performance, la méthode de réplication et le niveau de diversification géographique et sectorielle réellement obtenu. Frais (TER) des ETF ESG Les frais, ou TER (Total Expense Ratio), représentent un facteur clé pour tout investisseur à long terme. Même un TER de 0,20% peut, sur 20 ans, réduire sensiblement la performance finale en raison de l’effet cumulatif des intérêts composés. Les ETF ESG, souvent considérés comme “premium” en raison de leur filtre éthique, affichent parfois des frais légèrement plus élevés que les ETF classiques. Cependant, la concurrence pousse progressivement les émetteurs à réduire ces frais , ce qui profite aux investisseurs. Certains ETF thématiques ou très spécialisés, comme ceux axés sur l’eau ou les énergies propres, présentent des TER deux à trois fois supérieurs à ceux des ETF larges. Ce surcoût ne se justifie pas toujours par une meilleure performance ou une analyse ESG plus poussée. Il reste donc essentiel de comparer attentivement les frais et de ne pas se laisser séduire uniquement par le discours marketing. Performances des ETF ESG La performance reste un critère central, mais elle ne suit jamais une trajectoire linéaire. Les ETF ESG souffrent de l’idée qu’ils “sacrifiaient” du rendement au profit de critères éthiques. Au cours des cinq dernières années, il est vrai que la version ESG du MSCI World a légèrement moins bien performé. Plusieurs indices ESG ont nettement surperformé leurs homologues traditionnels. Par exemple, le S&P 500 ESG a progressé de 15,1 % de plus que le S&P 500 sur cinq ans. Il faut cependant se méfier des effets de mode. Un ETF performant sur 3 ans peut décevoir sur 10 ans si sa méthodologie exclut des secteurs qui finissent par rebondir. Il est donc crucial de comprendre la source de la performance : provient-elle d’une sélection ESG rigoureuse ou d’une forte exposition à la tech américaine, par exemple ? Méthode de réplication : physique vs synthétique La réplication est essentielle pour un ETF. Il existe deux méthodes : La réplication physique, où l’ETF détient vraiment les actions et qui rassure mais limite l’accès au hors-UE sur PEA. La réplication synthétique, permet de viser des indices mondiaux tout en restant éligible au PEA. Par contre, elle ajoute un risque de contrepartie et un manque de transparence. Avant d’investir, vérifiez toujours l’éligibilité PEA et la qualité de l’émetteur : la structure et le collatéral comptent autant que la performance. Diversification géographique et sectorielle La diversification protège votre portefeuille, mais l’ESG peut la compliquer. Un ETF ESG Monde offre une bonne dispersion, mais il reste rarement éligible au PEA en réplication physique. Les ETF synthétiques compensent ce manque, mais leur structure reste plus complexe. Les ETF régionaux (Europe, USA, émergents) permettent de personnaliser votre allocation, mais attention aux concentrations sectorielles. Par exemple, un ETF S&P 500 ESG reste très exposé à la tech américaine, même après filtrage. Un point souvent négligé : la corrélation entre ETF ESG. Deux ETF “verts” peuvent partager 80 % de leurs positions, ce qui limite la diversification réelle. Pour construire un portefeuille solide, combinez différentes approches, surveillez les recoupements et acceptez que la perfection n’existe pas. L’essentiel reste la cohérence avec vos objectifs, vos valeurs et votre tolérance au risque . ETF ESG : la conviction ne dispense pas de la rigueur Les ETF ESG peuvent permettre aux investisseurs d’ agir concrètement pour un impact positif , tout en cherchant à obtenir de bons résultats financiers. En choisissant des ETF qui appliquent des stratégies ESG précises, chacun peut bâtir un portefeuille en accord avec ses valeurs et ses objectifs de rendement. Atteignez vos Objectifs Avec les Objectifs, fixez vos projets (matelas de sécurité, achat immobilier, retraite) et suivez votre avancée, calculée sur votre patrimoine réel. Créer votre objectif Questions fréquentes Un ETF ESG est-il moins performant qu'un ETF classique ? Pas systématiquement. Sur cinq ans, le S&P 500 ESG a surperformé le S&P 500 classique de 15,1 % cumulés, tandis que la version ESG du MSCI World a légèrement sous-performé sur la même période. La performance dépend surtout de la composition sectorielle du filtre ESG, pas de la démarche ESG elle-même. Quel ETF ESG choisir pour investir en PEA ? Seuls les ETF ESG à réplication synthétique (comme l'Amundi PEA MSCI USA ESG Selection ou l'Amundi PEA Emergent ESG Transition) ou ceux répliquant physiquement des actions européennes (Amundi EMU SRI, Amundi CAC 40 ESG) sont éligibles au PEA. Les ETF ESG Monde à réplication physique en sont généralement exclus. Qu'est-ce qui différencie un label ISR d'un filtre SRI ou ESG Leaders ? Le label ISR est une certification française délivrée fonds par fonds après audit, tandis que SRI et ESG Leaders/Selection sont des méthodologies d'indice MSCI appliquant des exclusions et une sélection ESG. Un fonds peut suivre une méthodologie SRI stricte et obtenir en plus le label ISR, comme c'est le cas de plusieurs ETF Amundi cités dans cet article. Les ETF ESG thématiques sont-ils plus risqués que les ETF ESG larges ? Oui en général. Un ETF thématique (eau, hydrogène, énergies renouvelables) concentre l'exposition sur un nombre restreint de valeurs et de secteurs, ce qui augmente la volatilité et réduit la diversification par rapport à un ETF ESG Monde ou Europe large. Deux ETF ESG différents peuvent-ils faire doublon dans un portefeuille ? Oui : deux ETF ESG Monde de fournisseurs différents peuvent partager jusqu'à 80 % de leurs positions, car ils appliquent des filtres ESG proches sur le même univers d'actions. Combiner plusieurs ETF ESG larges n'apporte souvent qu'une diversification limitée. title: Telesat donates satellite capacity to support Venezuela’s recovery efforts | Telesat
body_text: OTTAWA, CANADA – July 2, 2026 – Telesat GEO Inc., a subsidiary of Telesat Corporation (Nasdaq and TSX: TSAT), one of the world’s largest and most innovative satellite operators, today announced the company is donating high-power satellite capacity to Top Comunications, a leading Venezuelan telecommunications company, to support disaster recovery efforts in Venezuela following last week’s devastating earthquakes. Top Comunications will use the high throughput capacity on Telstar 19 VANTAGE to enable faster restoration of critical communications infrastructure and support emergency coordination and public safety operations for government entities, first responders, and mobile network operators. “Satellite connectivity plays a critical role in the aftermath of a natural disaster like this one,” said Glenn Katz, Telesat’s Chief Commercial Officer. “This was an immediate way for us to contribute to the ongoing disaster recovery efforts with our partners on the ground, and we’re honoured to support Venezuelans as they work to recover and rebuild.”

Best Places to Visit in Kasol: Parvati River, Chalal, Tosh and More
summary: Discover the Best Places to Visit in Kasol, from the Parvati River and Nature Park to Chalal, Manikaran Sahib, Tosh, Kheerganga, and quiet village stops for a relaxed Parvati Valley trip.
body_text: Best Places to Visit in Kasol usually means more than one checklist stop. In this Parvati Valley village, you can move from the riverbank to a quiet forest trail, then end the day in a café lane or a shrine without rushing. That mix is why Kasol works for short breaks as well as slower 3 or 4 day trips. The guide below keeps the plan simple, covering easy sights, nearby villages, short treks, the best season, travel access, stay areas, and first timer tips. A Detailed Insight At Best Places to Visit in Kasol The Best Places to Visit in Kasol are easiest to enjoy when you keep the first day light. Kasol stretches along the banks of the Parvati River, and the old and new townships give you cafés, guesthouses, and river walks without making the day feel packed. Parvati River And Nature Park Kasol Parvati River is the main reason Kasol feels calm even when the market gets busy. The river runs beside the village, and Nature Park Kasol sits within walking distance of the centre, so it works well as a soft start for families, couples, and slow travellers. You do not need to plan a long visit here. Two to 3 hours is enough for a walk, a quiet sit by the water, and a few photos. It is best in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the crowds are thinner. Chalal Trek Trail Chalal Trek Trail is the easiest nature walk from Kasol. The trail starts from the small bridge near Kasol market, and most guides place the one way walk at about 20 to 30 minutes, which makes it ideal for a relaxed half day plan. It is one of the most rewarding places to visit in Kasol if you want quiet river sounds, pine cover, and a slower mood than the market side. Go in the morning for the walk itself or in the late afternoon if you want a café stop after the trail. Kasol Market And Café Culture Kasol market is small, but it is useful. You will find woollens, souvenirs, and simple shopping along with the café scene that has made the town famous with backpackers. Recent travel coverage notes that the Old Kasol to Chalal stretch has more than 40 cafés, with a mix of Israeli and Himachali food. This is a good place to spend a slow evening, not a rushed one. Sit down for lunch, walk the lane once, and keep the rest of the evening free for the river. For first timers, that balance matters more than trying to cover too much in one day. Places To Visit Near Kasol A short trip from Kasol opens up the rest of Parvati Valley places to visit. The best plan is to treat the town as a base and then add one spiritual stop, one village escape, and one trek or quiet hamlet depending on how many days you have. Gurudwara Manikaran Sahib Gurudwara Manikaran Sahib is one of the most meaningful stops near Kasol. Himachal Tourism places the gurdwara on the bank of the Parvati River and notes the hot sulphur spring inside the complex, which is also what makes the stop attractive to pilgrims and casual visitors alike. It is best for travellers who want one peaceful, spiritual break inside a scenic trip. A short road visit is enough for most people, and the stop usually fits neatly into a half day plan with Kasol market or a village walk on the same route. Tosh Village Tosh Village Kasol is worth adding when you want a village feel instead of another café stop. Travel coverage places Tosh about 13 km from Kasol, while tourism writeups describe it as a quiet end of the valley village with a slower rhythm and wide mountain views. It works best as a half day or overnight extension for couples, backpackers, and travellers who like longer hill views more than shopping. If your trip is only 2 days, keep Tosh as a backup. If you have 3 days, it becomes one of the strongest Kasol day trips. Kheerganga Trek Kheerganga Trek is the most ambitious name on a Kasol itinerary, but it needs the right timing. Current trek guides describe it as a day trek only, with overnight camping banned since July 2024, and they place the trek at about 12 to 13 km one way from Barshaini. It is best for fit first timers, regular trekkers, and anyone who wants a stronger nature day instead of a casual sightseeing plan. March to June and September to November are the most practical windows, while the monsoon and deep winter make the trail less comfortable. Kalga, Pulga, And Grahan Kalga, Pulga, and Grahan are useful when you want quiet village stays rather than more movement. Recent Kheerganga guidance recommends these hamlets as overnight bases before or after the trek, which makes them practical for travellers who prefer a softer pace and smaller crowds. These hamlets are best for slow travellers, backpackers, and people who want a quieter side of Parvati Valley. They are not the place for a long list of activities. They are the place to wake up slowly, walk a little, and let the valley set the pace. How Many Days You Need For Kasol For a simple trip, 2 days are enough for the river, Chalal, Kasol market, and Manikaran Sahib. That gives you a calm first look at the town without rushing from one stop to the next. It also works well if you are coming from a nearby city for the weekend. With 3 days, the Best Places to Visit in Kasol start to feel more complete because you can add Tosh or a longer village walk without dropping the easy stops. With 4 days, Kheerganga or a stay in Kalga, Pulga, or Grahan becomes realistic instead of rushed. Best Things To Do In Kasol The best things to do in Kasol are mostly slow and outdoors focused. Walk beside the Parvati River, spend time in Nature Park Kasol, cross into Chalal for a quiet forest walk, sit through a café meal, and keep one slot for Manikaran Sahib or Tosh. If you want a slightly fuller plan, add a village overnight or the Kheerganga trek, but only if you can start early and keep the day free. Kasol works best when you leave room in the itinerary instead of trying to force too many stops into one day. Best Time To Visit Kasol A practical Kasol window is March to June and September to November. Himachal Tourism classifies March to June as summer, July to September as monsoon, and December to February as winter in the Kullu region, while Kheerganga trek guides also prefer spring and post monsoon months. If you want easy walks, clearer views, and better odds of relaxed road travel, these months are the safest bet. Peak monsoon and deep winter can still be beautiful, but they are less predictable for short trips that depend on village roads and trekking plans. How To Reach Kasol The easiest way to reach Kasol is to fly into Bhuntar, which is the nearest airport in the Kullu area, and then continue by road. Himachal Tourism also notes that buses regularly ply to Kasol and taxis are available, so road access is straightforward once you are in the valley. For first timers, the most important tip is simple: avoid night driving in the hills if you can help it. Himachal Tourism’s safety guidance specifically advises against night driving, and that advice matters more in a valley trip where road conditions can change quickly. Where To Stay In Kasol Stay in Old Kasol if you want cafés, easy walking access, and a busy base for your first night. Himachal Tourism says Kasol has old and new townships, with more guesthouses, camps, and hotels growing around the village, so the centre is the most convenient choice for a first timer. Choose Chalal if you want quieter evenings and a riverside walk back to your room. Pick Tosh, Kalga, Pulga, or Grahan if your trip is trekking first and sightseeing second. Those stay areas are better when you want the village itself to be part of the experience, not just the road between stops. Travel Tips For A Smooth Kasol Trip Start early for Chalal, Tosh, and Kheerganga, especially if you are travelling on a weekend. The quieter hours are simply better for walking, and you will also have more room to enjoy the river and the cafés before they get crowded. Keep one full buffer in the plan for weather or road delays, especially if you are coming in monsoon season. Himachal Tourism warns travellers to stay careful near river banks and on hill roads, so keep movement slow and avoid making the trip feel like a race. Choose The Best Places to Visit in Kasol For Your Trip Style If your trip is short, keep it simple with the river, Nature Park, Chalal, and Manikaran Sahib. If you have more time, add Tosh for a village stay, or Kheerganga for a full trekking day that changes the feel of the entire trip. The Best Places to Visit in Kasol depend less on how many names you can fit into one plan and more on the kind of pace you want. Choose sightseeing, village hopping, café time, or trekking, then match the trip length to that rhythm. Frequently Asked Questions What Are The Best Places To Visit In Kasol For First Timers? The best places to visit in Kasol for first timers are the Parvati River side, Nature Park, Chalal, Kasol market, Manikaran Sahib, and one extra village stop such as Tosh, Kalga, or Kheerganga if you have enough time. Is Kasol Good For A 2 Day Trip? Kasol is good for a 2 day trip if you keep the plan light. Two days are enough for the river, Chalal, market time, and Manikaran Sahib, but not enough for slow village hopping plus Kheerganga. How Many Days Are Enough For Kasol? How many days are enough for Kasol depends on your pace, but 2 days cover the basics, 3 days feel balanced, and 4 days let you add Tosh, Kheerganga, or a quiet village stay without rushing. What Is The Best Time To Visit Kasol? The best time to visit Kasol is usually March to June and September to November because the weather is more suitable for walking, sightseeing, and short treks. Monsoon and deep winter can still work, but they are less predictable. How Far Is Chalal From Kasol? Chalal is a very short walk from Kasol. The main trail begins near the Kasol market bridge and usually takes about 20 to 30 minutes one way, which makes it easy to do even on a relaxed half day. Is Manikaran Sahib Worth Visiting From Kasol? Manikaran Sahib is worth visiting from Kasol because it combines a strong spiritual atmosphere with river views and the famous hot sulphur spring. It is one of the easiest and most meaningful side trips in the valley. Is Kheerganga Open For Trekking Now? Kheerganga is open as a day trek, but overnight camping is banned. Current trek guides say the ban has been in place since July 2024, so you should plan for an early start and a same day return. How Difficult Is The Kheerganga Trek? The Kheerganga trek is generally described as easy to moderate, with a one way distance of about 12 to 13 km from Barshaini. It is manageable for regular walkers, but it still needs time, stamina, and an early start. Is Tosh Village Good For A Day Trip From Kasol? Tosh Village is good for a day trip from Kasol if you want a calmer village atmosphere and valley views. It also works better if you are willing to spend part of the day on the road and part walking around the village. What Are The Best Things To Do In Kasol Besides Trekking? The best things to do in Kasol besides trekking are river walks, café stops, Nature Park, market browsing, and a visit to Manikaran Sahib. These are the easiest ways to enjoy the town without making the trip too tiring. Where Should You Stay In Kasol? You should stay in Old Kasol if you want convenience, in Chalal if you want quiet, and in Tosh, Kalga, Pulga, or Grahan if your trip is more about village life and trekking. How Do You Reach Kasol By Bus Or Air? You can reach Kasol by flying to Bhuntar and then continuing by road, or by taking a bus or taxi into the valley. Himachal Tourism notes that buses regularly ply to Kasol and taxis are available, which keeps the last leg simple.
